setting.world: Realistic historical England with no fantasy elements, governed by entailment, class hierarchy and marriage market custo
setting.description: Rural Hertfordshire and Derbyshire county society of landed gentry, clergy, militia officers and London merchants, centered on country houses, parsonages, assembly balls, and estates like Longbourn, Netherfield Park, Rosings Park and Pemberley.

characters.name: Elizabeth Bennet
characters.physical_description: A young woman in her early twenties with dark eyes and an intelligent, lively expression, light and pleasing figure with good symmetry. Typically dressed in simple Regency-era muslin gowns with long sleeves and hair styled up in curls.

characters.name: Jane Bennet
characters.physical_description: A beautiful young woman of about twenty-two with fair hair, soft blue eyes, regular features and a sweet smile. Slender and graceful, usually wearing elegant light-colored Regency dresses with her hair neatly dressed up.

characters.name: Mary Bennet
characters.physical_description: A plain young woman in her late teens with a serious, studious expression and spectacles-less plain features. Modestly built, typically wearing plain, high-necked Regency dresses with hair pulled back severely.

characters.name: Catherine Bennet
characters.physical_description: A teenage girl of about seventeen with a youthful, ordinary pretty face and brown hair worn in curls. Slight slender build, usually dressed in youthful muslin frocks fashionable for teenage girls.

characters.name: Lydia Bennet
characters.physical_description: A stout, well-grown girl of fifteen with a fine complexion, good-humoured countenance and light brown hair. Tall for her age with high animal spirits, wearing bright youthful Regency dresses and bonnets.

characters.name: Mr. Bennet
characters.physical_description: A middle-aged country gentleman with a lean face, sharp ironic eyes and graying dark hair. Of average height and thin build, typically wearing early 19th-century gentleman's coat, waistcoat, cravat and breeches.

characters.name: Mrs. Bennet
characters.physical_description: A middle-aged woman with faded former beauty, round florid face and fussy expression. Of medium stout build, usually wearing matronly Regency caps, shawls and fussy trimmed gowns.

characters.name: Fitzwilliam Darcy
characters.physical_description: A tall, handsome young man in his late twenties with fine tall person, handsome features, noble mien and dark hair. Athletic well-proportioned build, dressed in impeccably tailored dark coats, waistcoat, cravat, breeches and boots.

characters.name: Charles Bingley
characters.physical_description: A quite young, good-looking man in his early twenties with a pleasant open countenance, short light brown hair and cheerful expression. Of average tall height and easy build, wearing fashionable gentleman's blue coat, waistcoat and riding dress.

characters.name: Caroline Bingley
characters.physical_description: A fine, fashionable young woman in her twenties with handsome features, dark hair elegantly dressed and an air of decided fashion. Tall elegant figure, wearing expensive high-fashion London gowns, lace and jewelry.

characters.name: Louisa Hurst
characters.physical_description: A fine, handsome young married woman in her mid-twenties with fashionable dark hair and elegant features. Tall graceful build, dressed in very elegant and expensive Regency evening gowns with lace.

characters.name: Mr. Hurst
characters.physical_description: A middle-aged gentleman of fashionable appearance with a flushed, indolent face. Stoutly built with gentlemanly dress of coat, waistcoat and cravat, looking merely the gentleman of leisure.

characters.name: William Collins
characters.physical_description: A tall, heavy-looking young clergyman of twenty-five with a grave, stately air and formal expression. Large ponderous build with dark clerical coat, white bands, breeches and solemn demeanor.

characters.name: Charlotte Lucas
characters.physical_description: A sensible young woman of about twenty-seven with plain features, dark hair and an intelligent expression. Of average height and plain figure, wearing simple modest Regency muslin dresses.

characters.name: Sir William Lucas
characters.physical_description: An elderly, good-natured stout gentleman in his fifties with a baldish cheerful face and courteous smile. Portly build, wearing formal gentleman's coat, waistcoat, knee-breeches and presentation court manners.

characters.name: Lady Lucas
characters.physical_description: A middle-aged matronly woman with a kind, ordinary face and graying hair under a cap. Of medium stout build, wearing respectable matronly Regency gowns and shawls.

characters.name: George Wickham
characters.physical_description: A very handsome young militia officer with a fine countenance, good figure, bright smile and dark hair. Tall athletic build, wearing a red militia officer's coat with epaulettes, white breeches and boots.

characters.name: Mrs. Philips
characters.physical_description: A middle-aged, vulgar good-natured woman with a round cheerful face. Of short stout build, wearing provincial middle-class Regency dresses and caps.

characters.name: Mr. Philips
characters.physical_description: A middle-aged country attorney with a broad-faced, stuffy appearance and port-wine complexion. Stocky build, wearing plain dark gentleman's coat and cravat.

characters.name: Lady Catherine de Bourgh
characters.physical_description: An imperious, tall elderly noblewoman with a severe aristocratic face, sharp eyes and gray hair dressed high. Commanding stout figure, wearing rich dark silk gowns, jewels and lace head-dress.

characters.name: Anne de Bourgh
characters.physical_description: A sickly, thin young woman in her early twenties with pale insignificant features and thin sallow complexion. Small frail build, wrapped in shawls and riding in a little phaeton, wearing plain rich dresses.

characters.name: Colonel Fitzwilliam
characters.physical_description: A handsome young army officer in his early thirties with an open pleasant face and dark hair. Well-built military figure, wearing a red officer's uniform with epaulettes.

characters.name: Georgiana Darcy
characters.physical_description: A graceful teenage girl of about sixteen with pretty soft features, dark hair and shy downcast eyes. Slender womanly figure about Elizabeth's height, wearing elegant white muslin dresses.

characters.name: Mr. Gardiner
characters.physical_description: A sensible, gentlemanlike middle-aged man with an intelligent kind face and dark hair tinged with gray. Of comfortable middle height and respectable build, wearing neat London merchant's coats and cravats.

characters.name: Mrs. Gardiner
characters.physical_description: An elegant, sensible middle-aged woman with a pleasant handsome face and dark hair. Graceful medium build, wearing tasteful fashionable London dresses and bonnets.

characters.name: Maria Lucas
characters.physical_description: A young teenage girl with a fresh childish face and dark hair. Small slight build, wearing simple youthful muslin dresses.

characters.name: Mrs. Reynolds
characters.physical_description: An elderly respectable housekeeper with a kindly wrinkled face and gray hair under a neat cap. Stout matronly build, wearing a plain dark servant's gown with white apron and keys.

characters.name: Colonel Forster
characters.physical_description: A young militia colonel with a smart military appearance and becoming regimentals. Tall upright build, wearing a red militia uniform.

characters.name: Harriet Forster
characters.physical_description: A young, lively married woman in her late teens with a pretty flirtatious face. Petite cheerful figure, wearing fashionable bright Regency dresses and bonnets.

characters.name: Mrs. Jenkinson
characters.physical_description: A middle-aged lady's companion with a plain, fussing face and dowdy appearance. Thin nondescript build, wearing modest dark dresses and caps.

characters.name: Mrs. Younge
characters.physical_description: A middle-aged woman of genteel but disreputable appearance with a sharp painted face. Of average build, wearing showy former-governess dresses.

characters.name: Mary King
characters.physical_description: A young heiress with a plain, unremarkable teenage face. Small ordinary figure, wearing newly rich but unrefined Regency dresses.

characters.name: Mr. Denny
characters.physical_description: A young militia officer with a friendly ordinary face. Average military build, wearing a red militia officer's coat.

characters.name: Mrs. Long
characters.physical_description: An elderly neighborhood gossip with a commonplace aging face. Stout matronly build, wearing old-fashioned country gowns and caps.

characters.name: Mrs. Annesley
characters.physical_description: A respectable middle-aged gentlewoman with a calm pleasant face. Neat medium build, wearing modest genteel mourning-like dresses.

chapters.title: I
chapters.summary: The narrator ironically declares that a rich single man must want a wife. Mrs. Bennet informs her husband that Netherfield Park is let to a young, single man of large fortune named Bingley and insists Mr. Bennet visit him so he may marry one of their five daughters, while Mr. Bennet teasingly evades her, revealing his sarcastic reserve and her marriage obsession.
chapters.cover_description: Mrs. Bennet leaning forward eagerly gossiping in a cozy Regency sitting room at Longbourn while Mr. Bennet sits back dryly reading, the news of wealthy young Bingley taking Netherfield Park hanging between them.

chapters.title: II
chapters.summary: Mr. Bennet teases his wife and daughters by pretending he will not call on the new neighbor Mr. Bingley, enduring Mrs. Bennet's complaints about introductions and balls. He then reveals he has already visited Bingley that morning, prompting astonishment and rapturous joy. The family spends the rest of the evening scheming about Bingley's return visit, dinner, and dancing at the upcoming ball.
chapters.cover_description: Evening parlour at Longbourn with Mr. Bennet dryly revealing his secret visit to Mr. Bingley, while Elizabeth trims a hat and Mrs. Bennet and the Bennet daughters react in astonished joy.

chapters.title: III
chapters.summary: Anticipation for Mr. Bingley builds at Longbourn on secondhand praise after Mr. Bennet reveals nothing, followed by a brief call and a deferred dinner but reassurance he will attend the assembly ball. At the ball Bingley charms all and favors Jane while the wealthy Mr. Darcy is quickly judged proud and disagreeable after slighting Elizabeth as merely tolerable. The Bennets return home in high spirits with Jane distinguished by Bingley, as Mrs. Bennet praises Bingley to an impatient Mr. Bennet an
chapters.cover_description: A crowded Regency assembly ballroom at night, with Charles Bingley dancing joyfully with Jane Bennet in the center while Fitzwilliam Darcy stands aloof nearby coldly turning away from a seated Elizabeth Bennet watching him.

chapters.title: IV
chapters.summary: Alone after the ball, Jane confesses her admiration for Bingley while Elizabeth teases her universal goodwill and doubts his proud sisters. The narrator exposes the Bingley sisters as conceited heiresses of trade wealth and Bingley as an easy-tempered young heir impulsively renting Netherfield. Bingley's delight in the Meryton assembly and Jane contrasts sharply with Darcy's disdain, though his sisters concede Jane is a sweet girl.
chapters.cover_description: Jane Bennet in a white Regency muslin gown smiling sweetly while Elizabeth Bennet teases her in their candlelit bedroom after the Meryton ball, with Bingley's lively dance still fresh in memory.

chapters.title: V
chapters.summary: The Lucases of Lucas Lodge are introduced as intimate neighbours of the Bennets, with Charlotte Lucas as Elizabeth's close friend. The morning after the ball, the Lucas sisters visit Longbourn to dissect Bingley's open admiration for Jane and Darcy's proud slight of Elizabeth and Mrs. Long, debating pride until Mrs. Bennet's scolding of young Lucas over wine ends the visit.
chapters.cover_description: The Lucas family visiting the Bennets at Longbourn the morning after the Meryton ball, with Charlotte Lucas and Elizabeth Bennet gossiping over tea while Mrs. Bennet holds court.

chapters.title: VI
chapters.summary: Elizabeth observes Jane's growing but carefully concealed attachment to Bingley and debates with Charlotte Lucas whether Jane should display her affection more openly to secure him. At a crowded evening party at Sir William Lucas's, Darcy finds himself unwillingly fascinated by Elizabeth, watches her sing and refuses to dance, while Sir William's clumsy attempt to pair them is rejected by Elizabeth, and Darcy later startles Caroline Bingley by praising Elizabeth Bennet's fine eyes.
chapters.cover_description: Sir William Lucas grasping Elizabeth Bennet's hand to press her upon a stiff, surprised Mr. Darcy as a dance partner in a crowded candlelit Regency drawing room, Elizabeth pulling back in refusal while guests dance Scotch airs behind them.

chapters.title: VII
chapters.summary: Mrs. Bennet schemes to send Jane to dine at Netherfield on horseback in threatening rain so she must stay overnight and win Mr. Bingley, and Jane duly catches a bad cold. Alarmed, Elizabeth walks three muddy miles alone to Netherfield, astonishing the Bingleys and Darcy with her independence. She finds Jane feverish and confined to bed and remains at Netherfield to nurse her.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet arriving muddy and glowing from her three-mile walk across wet fields, dirty stockings and petticoat, standing surprised in the elegant Netherfield breakfast-parlour before the fashionable Bingley party.

chapters.title: VIII
chapters.summary: Elizabeth remains at Netherfield to nurse a still-ill Jane, enduring cold indifference at dinner except for Bingley's genuine concern. In her absence the Bingley sisters mock her wild muddy appearance and low connections while Bingley defends her and Darcy admires her fine eyes. Later Elizabeth joins the loo party with a book, sparking flattery of Pemberley and a sharp debate on accomplished women, before returning with news that Jane is worse.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet standing alone in the elegant Netherfield drawing-room at night in a simple mud-spattered muslin gown with untidy hair, holding a book while the fashionable card party watches her, lamplight glowing on the loo table.

chapters.title: IX
chapters.summary: Elizabeth stays overnight with the improving Jane at Netherfield and sends for Mrs. Bennet, who arrives with Kitty and Lydia hoping Jane will remain. In the breakfast parlour Mrs. Bennet embarrasses Elizabeth by flattering Bingley, sparring with Darcy over country society, and boasting of Jane's beauty and verses written to her. Lydia boldly extracts Bingley's renewed promise of a Netherfield ball once Jane recovers before the Bennets depart, leaving Elizabeth's family to be censured by the Neth
chapters.cover_description: Mrs. Bennet and her three daughters crowded into Netherfield's elegant morning breakfast parlour, with bold young Lydia confronting a smiling Mr. Bingley about his promised ball while a mortified Elizabeth blushes beside a coldly silent Mr. Darcy.

chapters.title: X
chapters.summary: In the Netherfield drawing-room Elizabeth is amused by Caroline Bingley's fawning over Darcy as he writes to Georgiana, then spars wittily with Darcy about humility, pride, and yielding to persuasion. After music at the pianoforte where Darcy watches Elizabeth and gallantly invites her to dance a reel, a jealous Caroline tries to mock Elizabeth to Darcy in the shrubbery, but he praises Elizabeth's beautiful eyes and she gaily escapes them, rejoicing that Jane is recovering.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth at the pianoforte turning music pages while Caroline Bingley performs and Mr. Darcy watches her intently from across the elegant Netherfield drawing-room in the evening lamplight.

chapters.title: XI
chapters.summary: After dinner at Netherfield, Bingley devotes himself openly to Jane while the rest of the party lapses into reading and dozing. Caroline Bingley fails to engage Darcy and instead prompts Elizabeth to walk with her, sparking a sharp, flirtatious debate between Elizabeth and Darcy on pride, vanity, and resentment. Feeling excluded and sensing Darcy’s growing attention to Elizabeth, Caroline breaks it off by calling for music on the pianoforte.
chapters.cover_description: A cozy Regency drawing-room at night with a blazing fireplace, where Elizabeth Bennet and Caroline Bingley take a turn walking together while Mr. Darcy looks up from his book by the fire, books and a pianoforte nearby.

chapters.title: XII
chapters.summary: Jane and Elizabeth attempt to leave Netherfield after Jane's illness, but Mrs. Bennet refuses the carriage until Tuesday and Bingley's entreaties delay them until the next day. Darcy, unsettled by his growing attraction to Elizabeth, resolves to show her no admiration and coldly ignores her. On Sunday the sisters finally return to Longbourn to a fretful mother, a quietly glad father, studious Mary, and Kitty and Lydia full of militia gossip.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet and Jane Bennet taking leave of the Netherfield party in bright spirits, stepping into a horse-drawn carriage outside the grand country house while Mr. Darcy stands aloof with a book and Miss Bingley forces a handshake.

chapters.title: XIII
chapters.summary: Mr. Bennet announces a visit from his estranged cousin Mr. Collins, heir to the Longbourn entail, shocking his family. He reads Collins's pompous letter apologizing for the inheritance, boasting of his patroness Lady Catherine de Bourgh, and proposing a week-long visit. Collins arrives punctually, tall and excessively formal, complimenting the daughters, admiring the house as his future property, and apologizing profusely at dinner.
chapters.cover_description: A tall, grave young clergyman in a black clerical coat bowing with stiff formality in the Longbourn dining-room while the five Bennet sisters and their parents watch over an admired dinner table, the hall and furniture he praises as his future inheritance glowing behind him.

chapters.title: XIV
chapters.summary: After dinner at Longbourn, Mr. Collins eloquently praises his patroness Lady Catherine de Bourgh, her condescension, Rosings, and her sickly daughter Miss de Bourgh, delighting Mrs. Bennet and amusing Mr. Bennet. Mr. Bennet draws out Collins further on his talent for delicate flattery to ladies, enjoying his cousin's absurd pomposity. In the drawing-room Collins refuses novels, begins reading Fordyce's Sermons with solemn monotony until Lydia interrupts with Meryton gossip, whereupon offended he
chapters.cover_description: Mr. Collins reading Fordyce's Sermons aloud with monotonous solemnity in the Longbourn drawing-room while Lydia interrupts him, with the Bennet family gathered around for evening tea.

chapters.title: XV
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins plans to atone for inheriting Longbourn by marrying one of the Bennet daughters, switching his choice from Jane to Elizabeth after Mrs. Bennet hints Jane will soon be engaged. On a walk to Meryton to escape Collins, the Bennet sisters meet the charming new officer Mr. Wickham, whose cold, colour-changing encounter with Mr. Darcy puzzles Elizabeth. At Mrs. Philips's the family secures an invitation to meet Wickham again over lottery tickets and supper, while Collins fawns over Mrs. Ph
chapters.cover_description: Two handsome young men facing each other on a busy Regency market street — a dark-coated gentleman on horseback gone pale staring down at a red-coated militia officer touching his hat — while a group of young muslin-gowned sisters watches in astonishment.

chapters.title: XVI
chapters.summary: The Bennet sisters and Mr. Collins spend the evening at Mrs. Philips's in Meryton, where Elizabeth is charmed by the handsome officer Wickham. Seated beside her at the lottery table, Wickham claims lifelong intimacy with the Darcy family and accuses Fitzwilliam Darcy of denying him the church living promised by old Mr. Darcy out of pride and jealousy. Elizabeth believes him completely, her dislike of Darcy confirmed, and returns to Longbourn full of indignation and admiration for Wickham.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet seated at a candlelit card table in a crowded Regency drawing-room, listening intently as the handsome red-coated militia officer George Wickham leans in to confide in her, lottery tickets scattered before them.

chapters.title: XVII
chapters.summary: Elizabeth tells Jane Wickham's account of Darcy's ill-treatment, but Jane refuses to condemn either man and suggests mutual deception. The Netherfield party delivers a personal invitation to the Tuesday ball, filling the Bennet household with anticipation, until Elizabeth's teasing question to Mr. Collins traps her into promising him the first two dances meant for Wickham and reveals his design to make her mistress of Hunsford.
chapters.cover_description: Bingley and his fashionable sisters paying a hurried personal visit to invite the Bennet family to the long-expected Netherfield ball, with the Bennet sisters glowing in anticipation of dancing, especially with Wickham.

chapters.title: XVIII
chapters.summary: At the Netherfield ball Elizabeth is devastated to find Wickham absent to avoid Darcy, and endures mortifying dances with Mr. Collins before being tricked into dancing with Darcy himself, where witty sparring turns bitter over Wickham. After Miss Bingley and Bingley, via Jane, discredit Wickham and Collins humiliates himself before Darcy, the evening collapses for Elizabeth as Mrs. Bennet loudly schemes for Jane and Bingley, Mary sings badly, and Collins clings to her. The Bennet party leaves la
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet in a simple Regency muslin gown forced to stand opposite the tall, dark-coated Mr. Darcy in the middle of a crowded candlelit Netherfield ballroom set, surrounded by dancing couples in evening dress and red-coated militia officers, tense and silent.

chapters.title: XIX
chapters.summary: The morning after the ball, Mr. Collins formally asks Mrs. Bennet for a private audience with Elizabeth and, despite Elizabeth's protests, is left alone with her. He delivers a long, pompous proposal citing clerical duty, his own happiness, and Lady Catherine de Bourgh's advice, offering to mitigate the entail by marrying a Bennet daughter. Elizabeth firmly and repeatedly refuses him, but Collins wilfully interprets her refusal as conventional coyness, forcing her to withdraw to seek her father'
chapters.cover_description: Mr. Collins in solemn clerical dress pompously proposing to Elizabeth Bennet in the bright morning parlour at Longbourn, Elizabeth looking distressed and amused as she tries to refuse him.

chapters.title: XX
chapters.summary: After Elizabeth refuses Mr. Collins, Mrs. Bennet tries to force her to reconsider, first by enlisting Collins and then by appealing to Mr. Bennet. Mr. Bennet settles the matter with ironic finality, siding with Elizabeth and reclaiming his library. Despite Mrs. Bennet's continued coaxing, threats, and complaints about her nerves, Elizabeth remains resolute while Collins soothes his wounded pride by pompously withdrawing his offer.
chapters.cover_description: Mr. Bennet seated calmly with a book in his shadowy Longbourn library, delivering his ironic ultimatum to a smiling Elizabeth while a florid, furious Mrs. Bennet stands beside them in cap and shawl.

chapters.title: XXI
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins punishes Elizabeth for her refusal with resentful silence and transfers his attentions to Charlotte Lucas, while Mrs. Bennet remains ill-humoured. After a walk to Meryton where Wickham explains he avoided the Netherfield ball to avoid Darcy, Jane receives a letter from Caroline Bingley announcing the whole Netherfield party has left for London. Alone upstairs, Jane is wounded by Caroline's claim that Bingley admires Georgiana Darcy and will not return for winter, while Elizabeth insi
chapters.cover_description: Jane Bennet in her shared bedroom at Longbourn, daylight from a window, reading aloud an elegant handwritten letter from Netherfield while Elizabeth Bennet listens anxiously beside her.

chapters.title: XXII
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins escapes Longbourn to propose to Charlotte Lucas, who accepts him for security and an establishment, to the joyful consent of Sir William and Lady Lucas. He returns to Longbourn concealing his triumph and hinting at a speedy return, baffling the Bennets. The next morning Charlotte confesses the engagement privately to Elizabeth, who is shocked and humiliated by her friend's pragmatic sacrifice to worldly advantage.
chapters.cover_description: Regency country lane outside Lucas Lodge in morning, a tall pompous young clergyman in black coat kneeling to propose to a plain sensible young woman in a simple muslin gown, the manor house visible behind them.

chapters.title: XXIII
chapters.summary: Sir William Lucas announces Charlotte Lucas's engagement to Mr. Collins, which Mrs. Bennet receives with disbelief, fury, and prolonged resentment toward Elizabeth and the Lucases while Mr. Bennet finds it amusing. A cool restraint falls between Elizabeth and Charlotte as anxiety grows over Jane, with Bingley absent from Netherfield and rumored not to return for the winter. Mr. Collins returns to Hertfordshire to court Charlotte at Lucas Lodge, leaving Mrs. Bennet tormented by visions of Charlot
chapters.cover_description: Sir William Lucas in formal gentleman's coat announcing Charlotte Lucas's engagement to Mr. Collins in the Longbourn sitting room, while Mrs. Bennet and Lydia react with incredulous rudeness and Elizabeth steps forward to offer polite congratulations.

chapters.title: XXIV
chapters.summary: Caroline Bingley's letter announcing the party's settlement in London for the winter extinguishes Jane's hope of Bingley's return, leaving Elizabeth indignant at his weak resolution and his friends' interference. Alone together, Jane insists she will forget Bingley and charitably defends Charlotte, Collins, and the Bingleys, while Elizabeth condemns inconsistency and selfish marriages. At Longbourn Mrs. Bennet repines, Mr. Bennet teases Elizabeth about being crossed in love, and Wickham's compan
chapters.cover_description: Jane Bennet pale and heartbroken reading Caroline Bingley's letter confirming the Netherfield party settled in London for winter, while Elizabeth watches in silent indignation in the Longbourn drawing room.

chapters.title: XXV
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins leaves Longbourn to prepare for his marriage to Charlotte while the Gardiners arrive for Christmas. Mrs. Bennet complains to Mrs. Gardiner about Jane losing Bingley and Elizabeth refusing Collins, and Mrs. Gardiner privately discusses Bingley's inconstancy with Elizabeth and invites Jane to London for a change of scene. During the week of social engagements, Mrs. Gardiner observes Elizabeth's marked preference for Wickham with unease, while bonding with Wickham herself over her forme
chapters.cover_description: A cozy Regency Christmas drawing room at Longbourn House, with Mr. and Mrs. Gardiner newly arrived from London distributing presents and fashion news to the Bennet sisters, while Mr. Collins in black clerical coat takes his solemn farewell in the background.

chapters.title: XXVI
chapters.summary: Mrs. Gardiner warns Elizabeth against an imprudent attachment to the penniless Wickham, and Elizabeth promises to guard her heart and discourage him. After Charlotte's wedding to Collins and departure for Kent, Jane's letters from London reveal Caroline Bingley's coldness and Bingley's absence, convincing Elizabeth the Bingleys have abandoned Jane, while Wickham transfers his attentions to the heiress Miss King, which Elizabeth bears with amused resignation.
chapters.cover_description: Mrs. Gardiner seated alone with Elizabeth in a Regency parlour, speaking earnestly and kindly as she cautions her niece against an imprudent attachment to Wickham, Elizabeth listening with lively intelligence in a simple muslin gown.

chapters.title: XXVII
chapters.summary: Elizabeth leaves Longbourn for Hunsford by way of London, parting fondly from her father and Wickham and enduring a dull chaise ride with Sir William and Maria Lucas to a joyful reunion with Jane at the Gardiners. At the theatre her aunt confides that Jane still suffers dejection over Bingley and has abandoned the Bingleys, while Elizabeth wittily defends Wickham's mercenary courtship of Miss King. The evening ends happily with Mrs. Gardiner's invitation for Elizabeth to join a summer tour possi
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth in a Regency muslin gown arriving by chaise in London and joyfully embraced by Jane at the doorway of the Gardiner house in Gracechurch Street, with Sir William Lucas and young Maria Lucas and eager Gardiner children on the stairs behind them.

chapters.title: XXVIII
chapters.summary: Elizabeth travels to Hunsford in high spirits after seeing Jane well, and is warmly welcomed at the Parsonage by Charlotte while Mr. Collins displays his house, garden, and prospect of Rosings with pompous formality. After dinner talk of Lady Catherine's condescension and Elizabeth's private reflections on Charlotte's contented management of her marriage, a commotion over Miss de Bourgh and Mrs. Jenkinson appearing in a phaeton at the garden gate ends with an invitation for the whole party to di
chapters.cover_description: Two ladies in a low phaeton stopped at the small garden gate of the Hunsford Parsonage, with Mr. Collins and Charlotte in attendance and Sir William bowing in the doorway while Elizabeth and Maria watch from the dining-room window.

chapters.title: XXIX
chapters.summary: Mr. Collins triumphs in a last-minute invitation for the whole Hunsford party to dine at Rosings, and coaches them in awe of Lady Catherine's grandeur. At the splendid, stiff dinner and afterward, Lady Catherine dictates and interrogates Elizabeth about her family, education, and age, while Elizabeth answers with composed wit that astonishes the company.
chapters.cover_description: A stiff, candlelit Regency drawing-room at Rosings where imperious Lady Catherine interrogates a composed Elizabeth Bennet, with her sickly daughter, fussing companion, and awed visitors arrayed around splendid furnishings.

chapters.title: XXX
chapters.summary: After Sir William leaves, Hunsford settles into routine with Charlotte cleverly keeping Collins at bay and enduring Lady Catherine's domineering inspections and twice-weekly Rosings dinners. Elizabeth escapes on solitary walks while awaiting Easter and Mr. Darcy's expected arrival. Darcy arrives with Colonel Fitzwilliam and makes an unexpected civil visit to the Parsonage, where Elizabeth tests him about Jane in London and notes his confusion.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth walking alone along a sheltered open grove edging the Rosings park, with the grand Rosings mansion looming in the distance and Miss de Bourgh's little phaeton passing on the lane beyond the Parsonage.

chapters.title: XXXI
chapters.summary: On Easter evening Elizabeth and the Collinses are finally invited to Rosings, where Colonel Fitzwilliam entertains Elizabeth with lively conversation that draws Darcy and Lady Catherine's attention. Lady Catherine dominates the talk of music with self-praise and lectures on practice, embarrassing Darcy with her ill-breeding toward Elizabeth. Elizabeth plays the pianoforte and spars playfully with Darcy about his pride at the Hertfordshire ball, while Lady Catherine interrupts to criticize her pl
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet seated at a grand pianoforte in the opulent candlelit drawing-room of Rosings Park, playing while Fitzwilliam Darcy stands beside her gazing intently at her, with Colonel Fitzwilliam seated nearby and the imperious Lady Catherine watching from her chair.

chapters.title: XXXII
chapters.summary: Alone at the Hunsford parsonage, Elizabeth receives an awkward solo visit from Mr. Darcy, their stiff conversation touching on Bingley, Netherfield, and the Collins marriage before fading into cold politeness. After Charlotte and Maria return, Charlotte half-jokingly suggests Darcy is in love with Elizabeth, but his silent, staring manner leaves them baffled as he and Colonel Fitzwilliam begin calling almost daily.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet alone in the Hunsford parsonage parlour, hastily putting away her half-finished letter in surprise as a tall dark-coated Mr. Darcy enters alone by daylight for an awkward morning call.

chapters.title: XXXIII
chapters.summary: While walking in Rosings Park, Elizabeth is repeatedly joined by the taciturn Mr. Darcy, then falls into conversation with Colonel Fitzwilliam on the way to the Parsonage. Fitzwilliam carelessly reveals that Darcy congratulated himself on saving a friend from a most imprudent marriage. Alone afterward, Elizabeth realizes Darcy separated Bingley and Jane from pride in their connections, leaving her indignant and ill.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet walking alone on a shaded park path at Rosings, clutching Jane's letter, unexpectedly meeting Mr. Darcy and then Colonel Fitzwilliam in red uniform, with the great house and Parsonage gate in the distance.

chapters.title: XXXIV
chapters.summary: Alone at Hunsford, Elizabeth re-reads Jane's gloomy letters and hardens her resentment toward Darcy for separating Jane and Bingley. Darcy unexpectedly enters and ardently proposes, but ruins his suit by dwelling proudly on her inferiority and family obstacles. Elizabeth coldly refuses him, accusing him of ruining Jane's happiness and cruelly injuring Wickham, and after a bitter clash of pride he storms out, leaving her weeping in shocked turmoil.
chapters.cover_description: A tall proud gentleman in a dark Regency coat agitatedly proposing to a stunned young woman in a simple muslin gown inside a modest country parsonage sitting room, her face flushed with anger and astonishment as he stands by the mantelpiece.

chapters.title: XXXV
chapters.summary: Still shaken by Darcy's proposal, Elizabeth walks to avoid meeting him but is intercepted at the park gate where Darcy silently gives her a letter and leaves. Alone in the lane she reads his long defence denying any renewal of his offer, explaining his separation of Bingley from Jane due to Jane's apparent indifference and her family's impropriety, and revealing Wickham's true history of squandered patronage and attempted elopement with Georgiana Darcy.
chapters.cover_description: A proud Regency gentleman in a dark coat silently handing a sealed letter to a young woman in a muslin gown at an iron park gate, with a grove and green spring park behind him on a bright morning.

chapters.title: XXXVI
chapters.summary: Elizabeth reads Darcy's letter, first angrily rejecting his account of Jane and Bingley and denying his charges against Wickham. Forced to re-examine the evidence of the will, the £3000 payment, Wickham's conduct, and Colonel Fitzwilliam's corroboration, she realizes Wickham deceived her and Darcy was blameless. Overwhelmed with shame at her vanity and prejudice, she accepts the justice of his reproaches about Jane's reserve and her family's impropriety, then returns home unable to think of anyt
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet alone on a secluded country lane, unfolding Darcy's long letter with a stricken, ashamed expression as the truth about Wickham and Darcy dawns on her.

chapters.title: XXXVII
chapters.summary: After Darcy and Colonel Fitzwilliam leave Rosings, Elizabeth endures condescending dinners and travel lectures from Lady Catherine while refusing to extend her stay. Alone on walks she memorizes Darcy's letter, torn between shame at her own prejudice, compassion for him, and grief over Jane's loss, her family's folly, and Wickham's true character. The chapter closes with fussy farewell directions from Lady Catherine as the Hunsford party prepares to depart.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet alone on a secluded wooded country lane near Hunsford, clutching Darcy's folded letter, head bowed in troubled reflection, with the grand facade of Rosings Park distant behind her in pale spring light.

chapters.title: XXXVIII
chapters.summary: Elizabeth endures Mr. Collins's pompous farewell civilities at Hunsford before Charlotte's entrance spares her. Elizabeth and Maria depart by chaise for London after leaving respects for Rosings, with Elizabeth hiding her private turmoil. Arriving at the Gardiners' where Jane looks well, Elizabeth is tempted to reveal Darcy's proposal but holds back for fear of grieving Jane about Bingley.
chapters.cover_description: Mr. Collins in clerical black handing Elizabeth into a waiting travelling chaise in the Hunsford parsonage garden while Charlotte and Maria look on, with Rosings Park looming in the distance.

chapters.title: XXXIX
chapters.summary: Jane, Elizabeth, and Maria return to Hertfordshire and are met at the inn by Kitty and Lydia with a boisterous cold luncheon, frivolous bonnet-buying, and news that the militia will soon remove to Brighton and that Wickham has escaped marrying Mary King. After a loud, Wickham-filled carriage ride home and a chaotic family dinner with the Lucases, Elizabeth resolves to avoid Wickham and Meryton, takes comfort in the regiment's imminent departure, and anxiously watches her mother press for a Brigh
chapters.cover_description: Two lively teenage sisters triumphantly showing off a cold inn luncheon and a new trimmed bonnet to their just-arrived elder sisters at an upstairs inn dining table, with bandboxes and parcels around them.

chapters.title: XL
chapters.summary: Elizabeth tells Jane of Darcy's proposal and refusal, then reveals his letter proving Wickham's villainy and her own prejudice and blindness. The sisters agree to keep Wickham's character secret to protect Darcy's confidence and avoid useless scandal, while Elizabeth hides Darcy's account of Bingley. At home Elizabeth sees Jane still loves Bingley, as Mrs. Bennet laments Bingley's desertion and gossips about the Collinses at Longbourn.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth confides in Jane the morning after Hunsford, recounting Darcy's shocking proposal and his letter exposing Wickham, the two sisters bent together in earnest, emotional conversation at Longbourn.

chapters.title: XLI
chapters.summary: As the militia prepares to leave Meryton, Lydia is invited to Brighton by Mrs. Forster, to Elizabeth's dismay. Elizabeth fails to persuade Mr. Bennet to forbid the imprudent trip, and at the officers' farewell dinner she coolly rebuffs Wickham's renewed gallantry and parts from him with mutual civility as Lydia departs noisily.
chapters.cover_description: Lydia Bennet in ecstatic farewell bidding noisy goodbye to her family at Longbourn as she departs with young Mrs. Forster for Brighton, while envious Kitty weeps and Elizabeth watches with anxious shame, with red-coated militia officers lingering in the background.

chapters.title: XLII
chapters.summary: Elizabeth reflects bitterly on her parents' unsuitable marriage and its harm to the daughters, then endures gloom at Longbourn after the regiment and Lydia depart. Her hoped-for Lakes tour with the Gardiners is curtailed to Derbyshire, and after arriving near Lambton she reluctantly agrees to visit Pemberley once assured Darcy is absent.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet in a simple Regency muslin gown riding in an open carriage with her aunt and uncle on a country road toward the grand Pemberley estate, with Derbyshire woods and distant great house in summer daylight, her face torn between curiosity and dread.

chapters.title: XLIII
chapters.summary: Elizabeth tours Pemberley with the Gardiners, admiring the house and hearing glowing praise of Darcy from his housekeeper Mrs. Reynolds, which unsettles her former prejudice. Darcy unexpectedly arrives a day early and, to her astonishment, behaves with perfect civility, seeks acquaintance with her relations, and asks to introduce his sister. On the drive back to Lambton, Elizabeth begins to vindicate Darcy to her aunt and is left alone to wonder at his altered manners.
chapters.cover_description: Pemberley House, a large handsome stone mansion on rising ground across a valley, seen from a wooded hilltop with river and trees below, with an open carriage approaching on the winding road.

chapters.title: XLIV
chapters.summary: Darcy brings his shy sister Georgiana and Bingley to call on Elizabeth at the Lambton inn, where Bingley's cordiality and tender memory of Jane reassure her and Darcy's humble attentiveness to the Gardiners astonishes her. The Gardiners become convinced Darcy loves Elizabeth and revise their opinion of him after hearing local praise and of Wickham's debts. Alone at night, Elizabeth's respect ripens into gratitude and affection as she contemplates Darcy's continued love and invites a return visit
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth in a modest Regency muslin gown at the window of the Lambton inn, flustered as Darcy's curricle carriage arrives below in the morning street, with her aunt and uncle watching her in surprise.

chapters.title: XLV
chapters.summary: Elizabeth, her aunt and uncle visit Georgiana Darcy at Pemberley, enduring an awkward, watchful reception from Miss Bingley and Mrs. Hurst eased only by Mrs. Annesley and refreshments. When Darcy joins them, Miss Bingley tries to embarrass Elizabeth with a sneer about the Meryton militia and Wickham, but Elizabeth's composure wins Darcy and Georgiana over. After the call, Darcy openly rebukes Miss Bingley's attack on Elizabeth's looks by declaring her one of the handsomest women he knows, while
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet blushing in embarrassment at a fruit-laden table in Pemberley's elegant north-facing saloon, as a tall dark-coated Mr. Darcy enters and watches her intently under the jealous stare of Miss Bingley, with shy Georgiana Darcy beside them and summer hills visible through open windows.

chapters.title: XLVI
chapters.summary: At Lambton Elizabeth receives two letters from Jane revealing Lydia has eloped from Brighton with Wickham and likely has not gone to Scotland to marry. Distraught, she confesses the disgrace to Darcy, who withdraws in gloomy silence, and she recognizes both her regrets over Wickham and her growing love for Darcy now seemingly lost. The Gardiners return, promise help, abandon the Pemberley visit, and hurry with Elizabeth back toward Longbourn.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet pale and in tears in a Lambton inn parlour, clutching two opened letters from Jane, as a stunned Fitzwilliam Darcy in dark Regency coat stands before her hearing of Lydia's elopement with Wickham.

chapters.title: XLVII
chapters.summary: On the road to Longbourn the Gardiners hope Wickham intends to marry Lydia privately in London, but Elizabeth insists he will not marry a penniless girl and blames herself for concealing his true profligate character. Arriving home, Elizabeth finds Jane alone bearing the crisis, Mrs. Bennet in hysterics fearing Mr. Bennet will be killed in a duel, and Mr. Gardiner promising to join the search in London. Alone with Jane, Elizabeth reads Lydia's thoughtless Gretna Green letter and learns of her fa
chapters.cover_description: A Regency carriage arriving at Longbourn House at dinnertime, with Elizabeth Bennet rushing past joyful jumping Gardiner children on the steps to embrace her tearful sister Jane in the entrance vestibule.

chapters.title: XLVIII
chapters.summary: While the Bennets wait anxiously at Longbourn, Mr. Gardiner reports from London that Mr. Bennet's search for Lydia and Wickham has failed and that Wickham has left massive gaming debts and no traceable relations. Mr. Collins sends a cruel letter urging Lydia be cast off forever, and when Mr. Bennet returns spiritless, he takes full blame for Lydia's flight before turning his guilt into bitter jests threatening Kitty with confinement from officers and balls.
chapters.cover_description: Mr. Bennet returned to Longbourn in philosophic composure, joining his daughters at tea in the dim parlour to confess his own blame for Lydia's elopement, while Kitty bursts into tears at his bitter jests.

chapters.title: XLIX
chapters.summary: An express from Mr. Gardiner brings news that Lydia and Wickham are found in London, unmarried but willing to marry if Mr. Bennet guarantees Lydia's settlement. Mr. Bennet and his daughters realize Wickham must have been bribed with a large sum, almost certainly paid by the generous Gardiners. While Mrs. Bennet erupts in delight over wedding clothes and gossip, Elizabeth and Jane reflect with mixed relief and shame on Lydia's narrow rescue.
chapters.cover_description: Jane and Elizabeth running breathless across the lawn after Mr. Bennet toward the little copse, with Elizabeth snatching her uncle's express letter to read aloud, Longbourn house behind them on a bright summer day.

chapters.title: L
chapters.summary: Mr. Bennet regrets never saving for his family and resolves to repay Mr. Gardiner for buying Wickham's marriage to Lydia, accepting a settlement that costs him little. While Mrs. Bennet triumphs shamelessly and plans finery, Mr. Bennet forbids the couple at Longbourn before being persuaded by Jane and Elizabeth to receive them. Elizabeth privately despairs that Lydia's disgrace has ruined any future with Darcy, as Wickham is to take an ensigncy in the North.
chapters.cover_description: Mrs. Bennet back downstairs at the head of the Longbourn dining table in oppressively high spirits, triumphantly planning fine muslins, new carriages and servants for Lydia's wedding while her family looks on.

chapters.title: LI
chapters.summary: Lydia and Wickham arrive at Longbourn for a ten-day visit, Lydia shamelessly exultant and Wickham easily charming while her family responds with sternness, mortification, and disgust. Lydia boasts of her marriage and precedence over Jane, while Elizabeth concludes Lydia loves Wickham far more than he loves her. When Lydia casually reveals Mr. Darcy was to have been at her wedding at St. Clement's, Elizabeth is left burning with curiosity and writes urgently to Mrs. Gardiner for an explanation.
chapters.cover_description: Lydia Wickham exultantly bursting into the Longbourn breakfast room, flaunting her wedding ring with a laugh while a stern Mr. Bennet looks on grave and Elizabeth and Jane blush in mortified shock, with Wickham smiling easily behind her in his red militia coat.

chapters.title: LII
chapters.summary: Alone in the copse, Elizabeth reads Mrs. Gardiner's letter revealing that Darcy secretly tracked Lydia and Wickham to London, bribed Mrs. Younge for information, and paid Wickham's debts and commission. Humbled and proud, she realizes her family owes everything to him. On her walk back she is overtaken by Wickham, trading veiled barbs about Pemberley, Darcy, and the Kympton living before parting with a forced brotherly truce.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet alone on a wooden bench in a secluded leafy copse, intently reading a long folded letter, her face caught between joy, shame and pride.

chapters.title: LIII
chapters.summary: After Lydia and Wickham depart for Newcastle, Mrs. Bennet is revived by news that Bingley will return to Netherfield. Bingley soon calls at Longbourn unexpectedly bringing Darcy, where Mrs. Bennet's vulgar civility mortifies Elizabeth and Jane, even as Bingley's renewed admiration for Jane becomes evident and a dinner is secured.
chapters.cover_description: Mrs. Bennet and her daughters crowded at an upstairs dressing-room window at Longbourn in daylight, watching Charles Bingley and Fitzwilliam Darcy on horseback riding up the paddock toward the house.

chapters.title: LIV
chapters.summary: After a vexing silent call from Darcy, Jane insists she will meet Bingley with perfect indifference. At the Longbourn dinner Bingley pointedly sits by Jane to Elizabeth's delight while Darcy remains cold and distant, and Elizabeth's hopes for private conversation with Darcy are thwarted by a crowded tea-table and a whist game, leaving Mrs. Bennet to exult over Bingley's attentions as Jane protests she feels nothing more than agreeable acquaintance.
chapters.cover_description: A crowded Regency dining room at Longbourn in candlelight, Charles Bingley taking his seat beside a smiling Jane Bennet while Elizabeth watches triumphantly and a grave Fitzwilliam Darcy sits distant and formal beside Mrs. Bennet at the far end of the long table.

chapters.title: LV
chapters.summary: Bingley resumes his attentions at Longbourn despite Mrs. Bennet's clumsy schemes to leave him alone with Jane, charming the family but delaying a declaration. After shooting with Mr. Bennet and another evening of maneuvering, he finds a moment alone with Jane by the hearth and proposes. The engagement is joyfully accepted by the family, with Jane revealing the Bingley sisters hid her presence in London, while Elizabeth quietly credits Darcy's consent and conceals his earlier interference.
chapters.cover_description: Jane Bennet and Charles Bingley standing close together over the drawing-room hearth in earnest private conversation, turning in surprise with glowing faces as Elizabeth opens the door, warm firelight illuminating a cozy Regency interior.

chapters.title: LVI
chapters.summary: About a week after Jane and Bingley's engagement, Lady Catherine de Bourgh makes an unexpected morning visit to Longbourn to confront Elizabeth over rumors she will marry Darcy. Alone in the copse, she demands Elizabeth deny the report and promise never to marry him, invoking Darcy's destined engagement to Anne de Bourgh and insulting Elizabeth's family, including Lydia's elopement. Elizabeth coolly refuses to be intimidated or to promise, ending the interview, and afterward conceals the true co
chapters.cover_description: Imperious Lady Catherine de Bourgh in rich dark silk confronting a resolute young Elizabeth Bennet with parasol face-to-face in a secluded green copse at Longbourn, tension crackling between rank and defiance.

chapters.title: LVII
chapters.summary: After Lady Catherine's visit to break off her supposed engagement to Darcy, Elizabeth is left fearing Lady Catherine will appeal to Darcy's pride and dignity and persuade him to give her up. The next morning Mr Bennet teasingly shows her a pompous letter from Mr Collins reporting Jane's coming marriage and Elizabeth's rumored illustrious match to Mr Darcy opposed by Lady Catherine. Mr Bennet laughs at the absurdity of Darcy as Elizabeth's admirer, while Elizabeth forces laughter to hide her hurt
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet alone in her room at Longbourn at dusk, anxiously replaying Lady Catherine de Bourgh's imperious visit to forbid her engagement to Mr Darcy, clutching at the fear that Darcy will be persuaded to abandon her.

chapters.title: LVIII
chapters.summary: Left alone on a walk from Longbourn, Elizabeth thanks Darcy for secretly saving Lydia, prompting his renewed proposal which she joyfully accepts. They recall Lady Catherine's failed interference, his letter, his humbled pride, Pemberley, and his confession to Bingley about Jane, returning home engaged and absorbed in happiness.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet and Fitzwilliam Darcy walking alone together on a country lane, Elizabeth looking up embarrassed as Darcy confesses his unchanged love, with open fields and Longbourn in the distance in soft morning light.

chapters.title: LIX
chapters.summary: Newly engaged to Darcy, Elizabeth endures an anxious quiet evening dreading her family's reaction, then confides at night in incredulous Jane until solemn assurances and the revelation of Darcy's aid to Lydia convince her. After a walk to Oakham Mount is arranged, Darcy obtains Mr. Bennet's consent in the library after Elizabeth earnestly professes her love, followed by Mrs. Bennet's rapturous delight at ten thousand a year and a newly easy day at Longbourn as Mr. Bennet rises in esteem for Darc
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet in a simple Regency muslin gown tearfully assuring her astonished father in the candlelit Longbourn library, with tall dark-coated Mr. Darcy waiting anxiously nearby among bookshelves.

chapters.title: LX
chapters.summary: Elizabeth and Darcy playfully discuss how he fell in love with her, crediting Lady Catherine's interference for hastening his proposal and his return to Netherfield. They announce the engagement by letter, with Elizabeth writing joyfully to Mrs. Gardiner, Darcy stiffly to Lady Catherine, and Mr. Bennet dryly to Mr. Collins. While Miss Bingley's insincere and Miss Darcy's sincere congratulations arrive and the Collinses flee Lady Catherine's wrath to Lucas Lodge, Elizabeth shields Darcy from vulg
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Bennet laughing joyfully beside Fitzwilliam Darcy at a writing desk in a Regency parlour at Longbourn, he holding a quill over a letter while she teases him, warm intimate courtship moment.

chapters.title: LXI
chapters.summary: After the double wedding, Mrs. Bennet revels in pride over Mrs. Bingley and Mrs. Darcy while Mr. Bennet delights in visiting Elizabeth at Pemberley. Jane and Bingley leave Netherfield for an estate near Derbyshire, Kitty improves with her elder sisters, Mary stays home, Lydia and Wickham live extravagantly and unsettled with help from their sisters, and Darcy and Elizabeth reconcile with Lady Catherine and Miss Bingley while remaining closest to Georgiana and the Gardiners.
chapters.cover_description: Elizabeth Darcy as mistress of Pemberley walking its grand grounds with Darcy, Georgiana, Jane and Bingley, with Lady Catherine's carriage arriving in the distance for reconciliation.
